title: 10 questions to ask any software vendor about sovereignty
summary:
Sovereignty is moving from buzzword to buying criterion. The European Commission’s proposed Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) would set assurance levels for the cloud and AI services public authorities buy, defining where data should live and who can access it. Parts of it could reach private entities too.

GitLab submitted its own comment on CADA because we share the goal of strengthening Europe’s digital sovereignty and security. We believe this important work should prioritize customer control, portability, interoperability, provider diversity, and risk-based safeguards. You can also view GitLab's submission on the European Commission's Have Your Say portal.

But regulation is only one lever. Many vendor conversations still don’t address sovereignty with enough depth. If this is a priority for your organization, here are ten questions I’d put to any software vendor, GitLab included. Use them as a simple assessment to confirm if a vendor takes sovereignty seriously:

10 questions to ask your vendors

1. Which layers of the stack do you operate yourself?

This question gets at ownership and accountability. A cloud provider and a software vendor control different risks, and a good vendor can help its customers appropriately distinguish between the controls it operates from those it inherits from the infrastructure beneath it.

2. Can I choose where and how the software runs?

Look for a vendor that offers flexibility around how you handle your data and architecture. Sovereignty needs to vary by workload, and the architecture should be able to meet your requirements. For example, self-managed deployments let you run software on your own infrastructure, whether on-premises, in a private cloud, or in a hybrid setup, so your data stays within boundaries you define.

3. Can I choose the AI models I use, and change them later?

Frontier models change fast, and your vendor should not lock you to one. Look for platforms that are model agnostic and draw on a diverse set of models and hosts. That gives your business the flexibility to use the best model for each use case as new ones are released. Open-weight models can often run in your own environment while offering strong price-performance.

4. Does my data train anyone’s model?

Data is valuable for training AI models, so ask for an official written policy around model training and request it includes sub-processors too. Consider it a great sign if the vendor can confidently point to resources that affirm they do not train generative AI models on your data and restrict AI model sub-processors from using both model inputs and outputs for training.

5. What data leaves my region, and why?

Personal data of identifiable users remains subject to regional regulations, like GDPR, regardless of its origin. However, some data and operational signals need to cross boundaries to keep service secure and available. The right vendor offers local hosting and can otherwise explain what types of data cross borders and justify why.

6. Who can reach my data, and from where?

Ask which roles can reach your infrastructure and customer data, from which regions, and under what safeguards. A vendor that offers deployment options with customer-managed encryption keys and private network connectivity adds further control over that access.

7. How do you handle data and risk classifications?

Ask how the vendor classifies different data and what governance mechanisms and incident response activities are in place to handle policy violations and security incidents. A clear classification approach also feeds data protection impact assessments.

8. Which independent audits cover the service I am buying?

Attestations such as SOC 2 Type II and ISO/IEC 27001 let a vendor prove its own layer separately from the infrastructure provider’s assessment. Check that the report scope covers the application you will actually use.

9. Can you match controls to the sensitivity of each workload?

Regulated industries require finer-grain policy controls. Ask whether the vendor lets you set the level of assurance workload by workload. This approach helps your team tune controls to the sensitivity of its function and data so you have speed with control.

10. What does leaving your ecosystem look like?

Portability and interoperability are sovereignty features. Ask how the platform connects to the other tools and models you use and how you would export your projects and history. The format of data exports is important; exports often yield datasets that are complex, poorly structured, or intentionally obfuscated, making them difficult to process without technical restructuring. A vendor confident in its product welcomes easy exports and open integrations.

Sovereignty helps organizations embrace flexibility

No vendor will give perfect answers on all ten of these questions, and requirements will continue to evolve, but the architecture you choose should be poised to absorb changes resiliently.

Teams get the most from AI when they can decide what their organization controls and how. That’s why GitLab believes customers should be able to choose which models they use and where they run. Take these ten questions into your next vendor conversation and see which vendors take sovereignty as seriously as you do.

If you’d like to see how GitLab measures up (we do!), review how we handle customer data and infrastructure in our AI Transparency Center.

title: GitLab Orbit is GA: Higher agent accuracy, lower token cost
summary:
An agent’s true cost isn’t only the tokens it burns. It’s the review that calls your code “safe to merge” after seeing the diff, but without any context on the pipeline. We call that artificial confidence, not artificial intelligence. Agents guess because code is all they can see; they can’t see the merge request that last changed it, the pipeline that ran it, the vulnerability it carries, or the people who wrote and reviewed it.

Guessing is expensive. If you’ve tried running agents in a large monorepo, one with tens of thousands of files, you know how it goes: the agent iterates, pinging the backend again and again for the information it needs to complete the task. Every round trip costs more time and more tokens. Eventually the agent gives up.

The model isn’t the constraint. Context is.

That’s the constraint that GitLab Orbit removes. Now generally available, Orbit is the context graph for your software lifecycle: a live, queryable view of all your code, merge requests, work items, pipelines, vulnerabilities, and ownership, with every relationship continuously updated as you ship. Every agent and engineer can work from one connected view of the lifecycle. In GitLab testing, agents connected to Orbit needed up to 45x fewer retries and used 4.5x fewer tokens on the same tasks with the same model.

Grounded agents get answers right the first time

An agent like Claude Code, connected to GitLab Orbit through MCP, stops crawling files and instead asks the graph. The first response comes back with real callers, recent changes, and owners, so your follow-up prompts can refine the answer rather than correct it. The difference is measurable. Compare the Market, one of the UK’s largest price comparison platforms, tested four context approaches for an internal AI code reviewer across 79 real merge requests. The GitLab Orbit-grounded reviewer matched about 70% of expected inline comments; RAG managed about 58%, worse than no added context at all.

“GitLab Orbit gave us an AI code reviewer that actually understands our codebase, not just the diff in front of it. We tested it against RAG and a few other approaches across real merge requests, and the gap was clear. Better comment placement, better summaries of what actually changed.”

— Ryan Harvey, Head of AI Engineering, Compare the Market

Fewer retries means fewer tokens

A recent analysis from a leading research and advisory firm found that the cost of an undisciplined agent session is dominated by retransmitting context that didn’t change between turns. That token cost comes from how the agent is set up, not from the model itself.

GitLab Orbit changes that engineering. The agent gets one bounded answer from the graph instead of reloading everything that might matter. In GitLab testing, agents connected to Orbit used up to 4.5x fewer tokens on the same tasks with the same model: each turn carries less context, and fewer turns go to work that never ships. Because the graph is shared, that cost doesn’t repeat per agent. Duo agents, Claude Code, Codex, and your own tools all query the same graph, so the context you build for the first agent is already there for the second.

Questions you couldn’t answer before

Since GitLab Orbit entered beta in June, we’ve worked with design partners running it against real codebases, real incidents, and real merge requests. Their first win was almost always a question they couldn’t get answered before.

Here are a few questions design partners asked Orbit that they couldn’t answer before, and what came back:

Which production services are exposed to this vulnerability? A single query returns the services that include the component, the merge requests that introduced it, the environments it reached, and the teams that own each one. One design partner answered a security-coverage question across 34 million entities in seven minutes; through the API, the same question would have taken half a day. When a vulnerability lands, security has a complete remediation plan within the hour, not a partial list by the end of the day.

What breaks if I change this? Before a push, a developer or their agent can ask which services, jobs, and environments a change touches, across every project in the group, not just the one open in the editor. Review agents bring the same answer to the merge request, so a “safe to merge” comment reflects the whole system instead of the diff. Across 79 real merge requests, Compare the Market’s reviewer flagged more real issues in the right places than their RAG-based version. Problems get caught in review, before they become outages.

Why does this CI job keep failing, and where else? GitLab Orbit shows how often a job fails across every project that runs it, which projects have drifted from the shared CI configuration, and who owns them. What used to be a Slack thread asking three teams “has anyone seen this?” becomes one answer. A financial services company used this to trace a build-system outage to a CI job failing 50% of the time, a pattern nothing else had correlated.

What depends on the thing we’re about to migrate? Every dependent service, job, environment, and owner comes back in one result. One design partner finished a multi-repository upgrade by asking the question directly: which projects are still on the old version? The last stragglers could be surfaced in one query with no spreadsheet or repo-by-repo audit to contend with.

Not every context graph can answer them

Context graphs are becoming a category, and most of them stop at code. GitLab connects the code change to the pipeline, the deployment, the vulnerability, and the owner, with your permissions intact. This means your team and agents can:

  • Start with a graph that already exists. GitLab Orbit draws on the data you already have in GitLab, which means there is no connector to configure, no ETL pipeline to maintain, and no second system of record to keep in sync. Enable it for a group and the graph is ready. A graph assembled from the outside takes months of integration work before it answers its first question. Orbit is also built to extend to non-GitLab data sources.
  • Index the whole lifecycle. GitLab is the system of record for the entire software development lifecycle, and GitLab Orbit connects it into one graph. Code indexes stop at the code. Work graphs stop at the ticket.
  • Keep your permissions without rebuilding them. GitLab Orbit mirrors nested groups, roles, and security-domain access. A graph that lives outside GitLab has to rebuild all of that and keep it in sync.
  • Give every agent and every engineer the same graph. Duo agents, Claude Code, Codex, custom tools, and the Data Explorer all query the same graph the same way. You invest in context once and every agent you add after that is cheaper than the last.

Bring the agents you already use

GitLab Orbit doesn’t ask you to change how your team works. The agents and tools you already run connect to one graph:

  • Agents on GitLab Duo Agent Platform query GitLab Orbit natively, with nothing to configure.
  • Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, and any other MCP-compatible agent connect through MCP or the GitLab CLI:
glab auth login
glab orbit setup
  • Custom agents and internal tooling connect through REST.
  • Engineers query the same graph through the Data Explorer.

Every path asks the same graph the same way, and the graph keeps up. GitLab Orbit indexes every push, merge, and deploy as it happens, so agents reason from the lifecycle in its most current state; at GitLab’s scale, that’s more than 1.5 million projects and 8TB of graph data in under 2 hours. Indexing runs as its own service beside GitLab, so however hard your agents use Orbit, GitLab itself never slows down.

Pricing: One shared query pool for your whole organization

GitLab Orbit is sold as query packs that form one shared pool sized for your organization. Everyone in your GitLab org draws from it, humans and agents alike, so usage flows between occasional users, power users, and the agents working on their behalf. Nobody requests access or gets assigned a seat. A query is one request to the Orbit graph, whether it comes from an agent (such as Duo Agent Platform, Claude Code, or Cursor), an experience built into GitLab, or the API.

Each query pack is $30 in GitLab Credits per user per month and adds 1,000 queries to your organization’s shared pool; usage beyond the pool is billed at 33 queries per GitLab Credit, about $0.03 per query. Promotional pricing is available this quarter for early customers. Contact your GitLab account team to learn more and size the right number of query packs for your organization.

Get started with GitLab Orbit

GitLab Orbit is now generally available for Premium and Ultimate customers, starting with GitLab.com today and reaching Self-Managed and GitLab Dedicated over the coming weeks. Customers can try it free for 30 days through their GitLab account team. If you’re brand new to GitLab, talk to our sales team about getting started with a GitLab paid plan, and we can help you add an Orbit trial as part of it.

Check out our documentation to help you get started.

title: GitLab Orbit: Find vulnerability blast radius without the manual hunt
summary:
A critical vulnerability needs a fix and a map. The fix is usually fast. Finding where the vulnerable component lives, who owns it, and whether it's exposed to the Internet is what costs you time. Most security teams piece that answer together from scanner reports, spreadsheets, and a Slack thread asking who owns a service nobody recognizes, and you stay exposed for every hour that takes.

GitLab Orbit, now generally available, replaces this manual work with a single query. Orbit connects code, merge requests, pipelines, security findings, and ownership in one graph that stays current as your teams ship. Ask which projects are affected and who owns them, and you get an answer in minutes. Agents answer from the graph instead of crawling repositories and stitching together API calls, so they need fewer retries and fewer tokens to get there.

Why scanners alone can't answer the question

PHP2Shell, the set of critical PHP flaws disclosed last week, illustrates the problem. PHP is usually installed as a system package, compiled from source, or baked into a container image, not managed as an application dependency. Vulnerable versions can sit on web servers, in container images, in old CI jobs, or in internal tools nobody remembers building. The fix was a version upgrade. Finding every affected installation took time.

Security tools provide different views of the environment. Dependency scanning identifies vulnerable application dependencies. Container scanning detects vulnerabilities in operating system packages, language dependencies, and other software components. Code search helps locate where images and configurations are referenced. But identifying a vulnerability is only part of the job. Teams still need to know which services are affected, who owns them, which pipelines build and deploy them, and where to apply the fix. That information is often spread across multiple systems.

That leaves your team to connect the dots, each holding a different piece. Your security engineer can assess the severity but may not see every affected system. Your platform engineer owns the base images and CI templates that hundreds of projects depend on, but can't see every project that uses them. Your developers get pulled off their roadmap to search repositories for a component they may not know they own. Your CISO has to tell leadership whether the company is exposed before anyone has a full list.

An attacker only needs to find one vulnerable system. You need to find all of them. Exploiting a vulnerability is now the most common way breaches begin, at 31% in Verizon's 2026 report, and the same report found attackers using generative AI at several stages of an attack. The map needs to exist before the advisory lands.

A first-party graph of your entire SDLC

Orbit draws on the data GitLab already runs on: your merge requests, pipelines, deployments, and vulnerabilities. A CVE in Orbit's graph connects directly to the services, pipelines, environments, and teams it touches. Because the graph is first-party, there's no second system to keep in sync and no new instrumentation to stand up.

Without Orbit, an agent or analyst can usually find the vulnerable code but not the full exposure. Someone assembles that picture by hand, tool by tool, and the gaps show up as the long tail of services nobody checked. With Orbit, one query maps the CVE to the services, pipelines, environments, and owners that depend on it, and the output is a scoped, prioritized list your security team can act on.

Agents without Orbit hit the same wall: they can't see the whole system, so they guess. In GitLab's testing on the same tasks with the same model, agents running through Orbit were up to 11 times faster, used up to 4.5 times fewer tokens, and needed up to 45 times fewer retries. During an incident, faster answers arrive while the team is still triaging, lower token use keeps queries across a large group from becoming a cost problem, and fewer retries mean your team can act on the first answer instead of re-running the question.

Watch the demo to learn how GitLab Orbit can help you understand your exposure:

One graph that connects a CVE to its owner

Blast radius is how far a vulnerability reaches: which projects contain the flawed component, how it got there, who owns those projects, and what changed recently. GitLab already holds most of those facts in separate places, and Orbit connects them. Turn it on for a top-level group, and Orbit indexes projects, merge requests, pipelines, work items, security findings, and source code into one graph of how they relate.

From there, you ask in plain language instead of correlating systems by hand: which projects use this library, which merge requests brought it in, and who owns each project? An agent traverses the graph and answers from indexed project data, and you can audit the graph queries behind each answer.

Access follows the roles you've already set, so people and agents see only what they're permitted to see. GitLab's built-in agents, including the Security Analyst Agent, use Orbit directly, and external agents such as Claude Code and Codex reach the same graph over MCP.

Contain your exposure quickly

title: What happens when vulnerabilities are discovered faster than you can fix them?
summary:
We're entering a new era of application security. Frontier AI models are uncovering complex flaws that traditional tools overlooked, and attackers are using the same models to exploit them faster. Remediation isn't keeping pace: Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report (DBIR) measures the median time to fully remediate a known-exploited vulnerability at 43 days, up from 32 in 2025.

Security teams are already stretched across growing application portfolios, third-party dependencies, and a steady stream of new disclosures. And while agents that find vulnerabilities and write fixes are becoming more accessible, integrating them into how enterprises actually build and ship software remains difficult.

A generated patch still needs to be tested. Security policies need to be enforced. Changes need to be reviewed and approved. And eventually, the fix needs to reach production safely.

This is where I believe the next major shift in application security will happen. We need to put autonomous agents to work inside the software factory. That's why we've brought Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5.1 into GitLab, and why we're connecting discovery, remediation, and prevention in one trusted workflow.

When critical vulnerabilities emerge, the clock starts ticking

Critical vulnerabilities like PHP2Shell send security teams scrambling to understand exposure. For a large organization, that means assessing impact across hundreds or thousands of repositories, applications, and dependencies.

Identifying exposure is only the first step. Teams then need to assess exploitability, prioritize affected applications, coordinate fixes, run tests, and get changes into production. Every handoff takes time, and speed is vital: 31% of breaches now start with vulnerability exploitation, the top initial access vector for the first time in the DBIR's 19 years.

As more critical vulnerabilities emerge, the traditional model of manually investigating findings, assigning tickets, and waiting for developers to write fixes becomes harder to sustain.

The time between vulnerability discovery and verified remediation needs to shrink dramatically. That requires security workflows capable of operating at machine speed, while preserving the controls organizations depend on to ship reliable software.

Bring agentic remediation into the software factory

AI agents can do impressive work in vulnerability discovery and remediation. The challenge is making that work reliable and repeatable across an enterprise.

An agent can generate a patch in seconds. Whether it understood the application, whether it validated the change against the real build, and whether it followed your security policies are separate questions. They get harder to answer, and more expensive to get wrong, as you deploy agents across thousands of projects.

At GitLab, we're bringing agentic security workflows into the environment where teams develop, test, and ship software.

Everything an agent does rests on how well it understands your system, and that understanding extends beyond the repository. GitLab Orbit, a live context graph of your software lifecycle, connects findings to the changes that introduced them, the pipelines that shipped them, and the teams who own the fix. It's also how you answer the questions that follow a disclosure like PHP2Shell: Are we exposed? Is it reachable? How far does it spread, and how do we fix it without breaking production?

GitLab Duo Agent Platform investigates findings in the context of your software and how it's built, filtering out likely false positives and prioritizing by exploitability and reachability.

For the findings that matter, Duo writes a fix and puts it through your pipeline to check for regressions and rerun security scans. In a single merge request, developers review the change, Duo's explanation, and the pipeline results.

Security teams move from understanding exposure to initiating remediation in one pass, and developers shift from chasing findings to reviewing fixes. Because these workflows run inside the software factory, agents operate within the same processes and controls that organizations already use to deliver software.

That's how we turn agentic security from an isolated capability into something an enterprise can trust and operate across thousands of projects, at machine speed.

Put frontier AI to work on the most critical vulnerabilities

Some of the most dangerous application vulnerabilities require a deep understanding of how software is intended to work: missing authorization checks, broken ownership logic, and business logic flaws that expose customer data or let users take actions they shouldn't.

Traditional scanners struggle with these issues because finding them requires reasoning about the application's behavior and the relationships between components.

Our new Business Logic Security Analyzer, the first GitLab capability to support Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5.1, examines how your application enforces its rules: it reads the whole repository and incoming merge requests, infers what each endpoint should enforce, and flags the gaps that pattern-based scanners often miss.

But the real opportunity comes from connecting those discoveries to the workflows teams already use. When a critical flaw is found, teams need to understand its impact, initiate remediation, validate the proposed fix, and ship it safely. Integrating frontier AI into the software factory creates a path to run that entire process at machine speed.

The intelligence of the model is only as valuable as your ability to act on it.

Prevent risky code from reaching production

Finding vulnerabilities earlier is valuable, and keeping vulnerable code and unsafe packages out of production altogether is even better. These protections become even more important as agents gain autonomy.

Security controls need to be embedded throughout the software factory and enforced independently of the people and agents making changes, with every change clearing the same gates before it moves forward.

GitLab Ultimate brings static analysis, dependency and container scanning, secret detection, policy enforcement, and approval gates directly into the software delivery process. Those policies are set centrally and apply consistently across projects and pipelines, so the author of a change, human or agent, cannot change or waive the controls evaluating its work.

The same scrutiny needs to extend to third-party software. Modern applications rely heavily on open source dependencies, and a vulnerable or malicious package can introduce serious risk before developers write a single line of code.

GitLab's Dependency Firewall blocks policy-violating packages before they enter your build. GitLab Secrets Manager lets each job access only the credentials it requests and is authorized to use, so a compromised dependency can reach only the secrets of the job it runs in.

Agents need the freedom to work quickly, within boundaries they can't cross. GitLab Duo Agent Platform gives each agent a composite identity that limits it to the permissions it shares with the requesting user, a sandbox that's destroyed when the task ends, and a record of every action. These boundaries are part of the GitLab Security Standard, under which agents earn more autonomy only as the controls at each stage are proven to hold.

The controls that make a change trustworthy need to hold at every step, even when the work happens at machine speed.

The next chapter of security will be defined by trusted execution

Frontier models will keep improving, security agents will get more capable, and vulnerabilities that were once difficult to discover will become easier to find. That progress will put enormous pressure on how organizations respond.

A security team can deploy the most advanced models available, but its ability to reduce risk will still depend on how quickly and safely it can turn findings into production-ready fixes.

This is why the software factory matters. It's where agents get the context needed to understand applications, where changes are validated against real builds and tests, where security policies are enforced, and where human oversight applies without slowing every step of the process.

At GitLab, we're bringing these capabilities together so you can automate remediation, uncover complex flaws, and prevent unsafe changes from shipping, all inside the workflows you already use.

The next security advantage will come from how quickly organizations can turn a critical discovery into a verified, trusted fix.

title: Extend GitLab Duo Agent Platform into your business systems
summary:
Developers mostly use GitLab Duo Agent Platform where they already work: the IDE, merge requests, and issues. But DevSecOps teams also support the business systems the rest of the company runs on, and those systems break too.

In Salesforce, for example, when a validation fails, a callout times out, or a null slips through a trigger, the error gets logged, but the log doesn’t explain the cause. An engineer still has to read the stack trace, find the class in the repository, check what changed recently, and decide whether this is a one-off or a regression. Meanwhile, the business user who hit the error has to wait.

When your Salesforce metadata lives in GitLab and ships through GitLab CI/CD, the code that explains the error is already there. In this tutorial, Salesforce calls a custom GitLab Duo Agent Platform flow through the Flows API the moment an error happens. The flow investigates the code, and your team gets a GitLab issue that already contains the root-cause analysis.

Along the way, three parts of the GitLab platform work together: GitLab Duo Agent Platform investigates the error, a GitLab issue tracks the work, and GitLab CI/CD runs the flow and ships the fix.

Salesforce is the example we’ll walk through in this tutorial, but the same approach works for any system that can make an HTTP request.

What you'll build

Salesforce makes one call to GitLab. A custom flow in GitLab Duo Agent Platform does the rest.

Errors reach GitLab Duo Agent Platform automatically from your Apex error handling, or on demand from a button. Either way, the same Apex job calls the Flows API, and the flow opens an issue with its analysis.

Prerequisites

  • GitLab Premium or Ultimate, on GitLab.com or GitLab 19.5 and later. The Flows API used in this tutorial is generally available from 19.5.
  • GitLab Duo Agent Platform turned on, with custom flows allowed for your top-level group.
  • Your Salesforce metadata (Apex classes, triggers, Flows) stored in a GitLab project. This is the project the flow will read.
  • A Maintainer or Owner role in that project.
  • In Salesforce, permission to create a Named Credential, a custom metadata type, and Apex classes.
  • Your Salesforce deployments must be running through a GitLab CI/CD pipeline, so the fix can ship from the same issue.

Step 1: Write the triage flow

Start in GitLab, because Salesforce will need the flow's ID later.

A custom flow is one YAML file in the flow registry v1 syntax. This one has a single agent. When Salesforce starts the flow, it sends the error details as the flow's goal. The agent reads them as context:goal, investigates the repository, and opens one issue.

version: "v1"
environment: ambient

components:
  - name: "sf_error_triage"
    type: AgentComponent
    prompt_id: "sf_error_triage_prompt"
    inputs:
      - from: "context:project_id"
        as: "project_id"
      - from: "context:goal"
        as: "error_report"
    toolset:
      - "find_files"      # locate the class or Flow in the repository
      - "grep"
      - "read_file"
      - "list_commits"    # find recent changes to that file
      - "create_issue"    # the only write: open the triage issue

prompts:
  - prompt_id: "sf_error_triage_prompt"
    prompt_template:
      system: |
        You triage Salesforce runtime errors for a team that keeps its
        Salesforce metadata (Apex classes, triggers, Flows) in this project.

        You receive an error report with a class name, exception type,
        message and stack trace.

        1. Find the source file for the class or Flow named in the report.
        2. Read the code around the lines in the stack trace.
        3. List recent commits that touched that file and identify any change
           that plausibly introduced the error.
        4. Create one issue:
           - Title: "[Salesforce error]  in "
           - Label: salesforce-error
           - Description: the original error, then sections for
             Likely cause, Affected component, Suspect change,
             Suggested next step, and Confidence (high, medium or low,
             with one line of reasoning).

        Rules:
        - Cite file paths, line numbers and commit SHAs for every claim.
        - If you cannot find the code or a suspect commit, say so. Do not guess.
        - Do not change code. A person decides what happens next.
      user: |
        Project ID: {{project_id}}
        Error report:
        {{error_report}}
      placeholder: history

routers:
  - from: "sf_error_triage"
    to: "end"

flow:
  entry_point: "sf_error_triage"

The toolset is deliberately narrow: four tools read and one creates an issue. The flow can't push code or change existing issues, which makes it easy to review and easy to trust.

Two lines in the prompt do the most work. Requiring a citation for every claim lets an engineer check the reasoning in a minute. Allowing "not found" stops the agent from inventing a cause.

To create the flow, go to your project, select AI > Flows > New flow, choose Flow, paste the YAML, and select Create flow. You can also build and test it in VS Code with the GitLab flow builder.

Step 2: Enable the flow and get its consumer ID

A flow must be enabled in a project before anything can run it.

  1. In your project, select AI > Flows, open the Managed tab, and select your flow.
  2. Select Enable and choose the project that holds your Salesforce code. GitLab creates a service account for the flow, named ai--. The flow runs with a composite identity, so it can never access more than the user who starts it. When Salesforce starts the flow through the API, GitLab runs it as this service account.
  3. You don't need a mention or assign trigger. Salesforce will start this flow through the API.

To start a custom flow through the API, Salesforce passes the flow's ai_catalog_item_consumer_id. Look it up with a short GraphQL query from the docs, and use the number at the end of the returned gid://gitlab/AiCatalogItemConsumer/. Note it, along with the project ID.

Finally, create a project access token with the api scope and at least the Developer role. Salesforce will use it to call GitLab. With a lower role, the API refuses to run catalog flows.

Step 3: Call the flow from Salesforce

Store the token in a Named Credential. Create a Named Credential called GitLab_API with the URL https://gitlab.com, backed by an External Credential that sends your project access token in the PRIVATE-TOKEN header. The token never appears in code.

Call the Flows API from a Queueable. Salesforce doesn't allow callouts in the middle of saving a record, so the call runs as a background job. The job turns the exception into the flow's goal and starts the flow:

public with sharing class DuoTriageJob implements Queueable, Database.AllowsCallouts {
    private final String goal;

    public DuoTriageJob(Exception e, String className) {
        goal = 'Class: ' + className
            + '\nException: ' + e.getTypeName()
            + '\nMessage: ' + e.getMessage()
            + '\nStack trace:\n' + e.getStackTraceString();
    }

    public void execute(QueueableContext ctx) {
        Duo_Triage_Setting__mdt cfg = Duo_Triage_Setting__mdt.getInstance('Default');

        HttpRequest req = new HttpRequest();
        req.setEndpoint('callout:GitLab_API/api/v4/ai/duo_workflows/workflows');
        req.setMethod('POST');
        req.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
        req.setBody(JSON.serialize(new Map{
            'project_id'                    => cfg.Project_Id__c,
            'ai_catalog_item_consumer_id'   => cfg.Consumer_Id__c.intValue(),
            'goal'                          => goal,
            'start_workflow'                => true,
            'allow_agent_to_request_user'   => false,
            'agent_privileges'              => new List{ 1, 2, 3 },
            'pre_approved_agent_privileges' => new List{ 1, 2, 3 }
        }));
        HttpResponse res = new Http().send(req);
        // 201 Created: the response includes web_url, a link to the agent session.
    }
}

title: Pillow CVE-2026-112900: How to find and fix it with GitLab
summary:
GitLab is not affected by CVE-2026-112900 or the other vulnerabilities fixed in Pillow 13.0.0. GitLab products do not include the Pillow library, and our Security team has found no evidence of impact to GitLab-managed infrastructure. GitLab.com, GitLab Self-Managed, and GitLab Dedicated are not impacted.

Pillow is one of the most widely used image libraries in the Python ecosystem. It often sits several layers down in a dependency tree, pulled in by a web framework, a thumbnailing service or an ML toolkit that nobody chose it for directly. On October 16, 2026, the Pillow project released version 13.0.0, and one of its security fixes is CVE-2026-112900: an argument injection in the way Pillow calls Ghostscript to render EPS images. The CVE record, published on October 19, rates it 9.2 (Critical) on CVSS 4.0. It affects every Pillow release from 2.6.0 up to, but not including, 13.0.0. No exploitation in the wild has been reported so far, but CISA's assessment marks it as automatable with total technical impact.

Upgrade Pillow to 13.0.0 on every project and image that handles untrusted images, and remove Ghostscript from images that do not need EPS support.

This guide is for security and platform teams with Python projects on GitLab. It covers the fixed version for each distribution, how the flaw works, the other High and Critical issues fixed in the same release, how to locate affected projects with dependency scanning, container scanning, GitLab Orbit, and code search, and how to remediate at scale with GitLab Duo Agent Platform.

CVE-2026-112900 at a glance

CVE-2026-112900 is an OS command and argument injection flaw in Pillow's EPS plugin, rated Critical (CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2) by the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA). The CVE record was published on October 19, 2026.

FieldDetail
CVECVE-2026-112900
GitHub advisoryGHSA-w889-685w-c8fh
TitlePillow: Argument Injection in Ghostscript call, potentially leading into RCE
WeaknessCWE-88 (argument injection), CWE-78 (OS command injection)
CVSS 4.09.2 Critical (AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H)
Affected versionsPillow >= 2.6.0 and < 13.0.0
Fixed inPillow 13.0.0
Exploitation statusNone known at the time of writing (CISA SSVC assessment dated October 20, 2026)

Upgrade Pillow to a fixed version now

Upgrade Pillow to 13.0.0 or later. The CVE record lists 13.0.0 as the only fixed version, so every older branch needs to move to it. Framework updates and input validation on image contents do not help here, because the flaw is in how the filename reaches Ghostscript.

Your Python versionWhat to do
3.11 to 3.15Upgrade with pip install --upgrade "pillow>=13.0.0", or raise the pin in your lockfile or requirements file.

If your Pillow comes from a distribution package, check the distribution's tracker first. Distribution packages keep their own version numbers, so compare against the tracker instead of pip show. Status as of October 26, 2026:

DistributionPillow package versionStatus
Debian 12 (bookworm)9.4.0-1.1+deb12u1Vulnerable, no fix yet
Debian 13 (trixie)11.1.0-5+deb13u4Vulnerable, no fix yet
Debian forky (testing)12.3.0-1Vulnerable, no fix yet
Debian sid (unstable)13.0.0-1Fixed
SUSE Linux Enterprise (Server 15 SP4 to SP7 and 16.0 to 16.2, among others) and openSUSE Leap 16.0 and 16.1python-PillowAffected, no fix listed
Amazon Linux 2023 and 2027 Previewpython-pillowPending fix

Sources: Debian, SUSE and Amazon Linux security trackers, as of October 26, 2026. Amazon Linux 2 is listed as not affected. Ubuntu lists all releases as needing evaluation, and Red Hat, Arch Linux and Oracle Linux had no record for this CVE. Alpine's tracker could not be checked.

Until your distribution ships a fix, install Pillow 13.0.0 from PyPI in a virtual environment or container, or apply the workarounds below.

Rebuild your container images. If your Dockerfile installs Pillow without pinning a patch version, rebuild it with docker build --pull --no-cache and redeploy it so the install step resolves the fixed release. Images that pin a version, such as pillow==12.3.0, need the pin changed first. Images built on top of other base images only get the fix once their maintainers update them, so check the upstream image before you rebuild.

Pillow 13.0.0 also changes a few behaviors, such as how duplicate TIFF tags are handled and how I-mode images are saved as PNG, so run your image-processing tests before you ship the upgrade.

How the vulnerability works

EPS files are PostScript programs, so Pillow shells out to Ghostscript (gs) to render them, passing the input filename right after -f with no sanitizing.

When the image object has a .name that exists on disk, Pillow used that name as-is. Ghostscript's argument parser gives two kinds of strings special meaning:

  • A leading - is read as an option rather than a filename, which gives an attacker argument injection (CWE-88).
  • A leading @ tells Ghostscript to read more command-line arguments from the named text file. If the attacker also controls that file's contents, they control additional Ghostscript arguments, which is the path toward command execution (CWE-78).

The advisory notes that this works even with -dSAFER, the sandbox flag Pillow passes by default. That flag restricts what a PostScript program can do, but it does not stop an attacker from injecting arguments into the command line itself.

How to check if you are affected

You are exposed only if all of these are true:

  1. Pillow is below 13.0.0.
  2. Ghostscript is installed.
  3. Your code opens an EPS file by a filename an attacker can influence, such as an upload saved under its original name.
  4. The image is loaded or rendered, not just opened.

Full command execution also needs the attacker to control a text file referenced with a leading @. Services that generate their own filenames or use in-memory streams are far less likely to be reachable.

If you cannot upgrade yet: save uploads under generated names, restrict formats with Image.open(f, formats=["PNG", "JPEG"]), or remove Ghostscript from images that do not need it.

It's not just one bug: Every High and Critical issue in 13.0.0

The 13.0.0 release notes list 17 High and Critical advisories (3 Critical, 14 High). Fifteen of them map to a CVE. The two that do not, GHSA-xcvg-w56q-r89m and GHSA-78g4-xqwv-q3g8, are worth watching, because tools that match only on CVE IDs would miss them.

Locate Pillow across your GitLab groups

Find every project that installs Pillow, then fix first the ones that also have Ghostscript and accept uploads.

  1. Dependency scanning reports the Pillow version in your lockfiles, including transitive dependencies. Turn it on per project, or for a whole group with a scan execution policy. Merge request approval policies can block merges that add a vulnerable version, and continuous vulnerability scanning re-checks existing projects when an advisory is published, for advisories up to 14 days old.

  1. Container scanning finds Ghostscript installed as an OS package. Images with Pillow but no Ghostscript cannot render EPS files, so they are lower priority. It misses Ghostscript compiled from source. Turn container scanning on the same way.
  2. GitLab Orbit: Because Pillow tends to arrive as someone else's dependency, asking "who uses it?" is hard from any single project. GitLab Orbit turns your projects, pipelines, security findings and code into a graph that an agent can query. Enable it on the top-level group, then ask for the Python projects that handle images and for the projects with open findings on CVE-2026-112900 or the other Pillow advisories. EPS files are PostScript programs, so Pillow shells out to Ghostscript (gs) to render them, passing the input filename right after -f with no sanitizing.

title: PHP2Shell: GitLab helps find and remediate critical PHP flaws
summary:
GitLab is not affected by PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). The GitLab application is not written in PHP and does not run it to serve web requests, and our Security team has found no evidence of impact to GitLab-managed infrastructure. GitLab.com, GitLab Self-Managed, and GitLab Dedicated are not impacted.

PHP is a widely used programming language that runs on web servers and powers popular platforms like WordPress, Drupal, and Magento, so a flaw in PHP itself can affect many websites and applications. On October 21, 2026, the PHP project fixed two critical remote code execution flaws in PHP, together known as PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). PHP rates both 9.2 on CVSS v4.0. The flaws are in the PHP engine, not in any framework, library, or application code, so there is no application-level fix. Any web server that runs PHP is affected, including NGINX and Apache. The PHP project confirmed the vulnerability on Apache with mod_php, where an unauthenticated request can achieve remote code execution before any application code runs.

Upgrade every server and container that runs PHP to serve web requests to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, or to your distribution’s patched package now.

This guide is for security and platform teams with PHP projects on GitLab. It covers the fixed version for each PHP branch and distribution, how to use GitLab features to locate PHP projects across your groups, how to track remediation, and how to check for signs of compromise.

Upgrade PHP to a fixed version now

Upgrade the PHP runtime on every host and in every container image to a fixed version. Framework updates, Composer updates, input validation, and authentication don’t help, because PHP handles the request before application code runs.

BranchFixed in
PHP 8.5.x8.5.12
PHP 8.4.x8.4.27
PHP 8.3.x8.3.36
PHP 8.2.x8.2.35 (end of life December 31, 2026)
PHP 8.6 release candidates8.6.0RC4. The official php:8.6-rc image was still on RC3 on October 21, and RC3 does not have the fix.
PHP 8.1 and olderNo official release. PHP published minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1, and some distributions ship patched packages.

If your PHP comes from a distribution package, upgrade that package. Fixed package versions as of October 22:

DistributionFixed package
Ubuntu 26.04php8.5 8.5.4-0ubuntu1.5
Ubuntu 24.04php8.3 8.3.6-0ubuntu0.24.04.13
Ubuntu 22.04php8.1 8.1.2-1ubuntu2.28
Debian 13php8.4 8.4.27-1~deb13u1
Debian 12php8.2 8.2.35-1~deb12u1
Alpine 3.24php83 8.3.36, php84 8.4.27, php85 8.5.12
RHEL 10php 8.3.36-1.el10_2 (RHSA-2026:87070), php8.4 8.4.27-1.el10_2 (RHSA-2026:87071)
RHEL 9php 8.0.30-8.el9_8.1 (RHSA-2026:87151), php:8.2 8.2.35-1 (RHSA-2026:87072), php:8.3 8.3.36-1 (RHSA-2026:87079); php:8.4 had no fix yet on October 22
RHEL 8php:7.4 7.4.33-8 (RHSA-2026:87080); check Red Hat’s CVE pages for php:8.2. Retired streams (7.2, 7.3, 8.0) get no fix

Sources: Ubuntu, Debian, Alpine, and Red Hat security trackers, as of October 22, 2026.

Ubuntu, and Red Hat for its 7.4 and 8.0 packages, keep the old upstream version number and backport the fix. Compare the package versions rather than php -v. Restart every process that runs PHP after upgrading.

Rebuild your container images. If your image uses a floating tag of the official php image, such as php:8, php:8.3, php:8.3-apache or php:latest, rebuild it with docker build --pull and redeploy it. Images that pin a patch version, such as php:8.3.35-apache, need the tag changed to the fixed version first. Images built on derivatives such as wordpress or drupal get the fix only after their maintainers publish an updated image, so check the upstream image before you rebuild.

Locate PHP projects across your GitLab groups

Any project that runs PHP to serve web requests needs a fixed version, including the ones that are easy to forget, such as an internal dashboard, a marketing site, or a CI job image. Finding them takes two views: a static search of what your repositories declare and your images contain, and a runtime inventory of what actually runs. GitLab covers the static view with three features. Use them in this order.

1. Container scanning

Container scanning reports vulnerabilities in operating system packages, so it finds PHP installed with apt, apk, or dnf, and it reports the two CVEs once they reach the scanner's vulnerability database. To turn it on for a project, add the template to .gitlab-ci.yml:

include:
  - template: Security/Container-Scanning.gitlab-ci.yml

container_scanning:
  variables:
    # Experimental, Ultimate only: also reports runtimes not installed by a package manager
    CS_BINARY_SCAN: "true"

You can also use a group-level scan execution policy to turn container scanning on for every project in a group at once. When a policy is enabled, the next time a pipeline is run, it will be run with container scanning. Container scanning results for the default branch can be reviewed in the Vulnerability Report after the scanner completes.

Additionally, you can set up Merge Request Approval policies with container scanning. With merge request approvals in play, if a code change contains PHP2Shell, the policy will block a merge without approval from the selected parties.

By default, container scanning detects only PHP installed as a package. The official images compile it from source, leaving no package record, so a project can pass container scanning and still run a vulnerable version.

Container scanning analyzer 8.7.0, released on October 29, adds an experimental binary scan that reports runtimes installed without a package manager, which closes that gap. It is available on Ultimate and off by default: set CS_BINARY_SCAN to "true" to turn it on. If you leave it off, Orbit and code search below cover it.

2. GitLab Orbit

GitLab Orbit indexes your projects, pipelines, security findings, and source code, including PHP, into a queryable graph, so you can ask an agent to review an entire group. With Orbit enabled on the top-level group, an agent can list every project that contains PHP code, including the projects that compile PHP or use the official php images, which container scanning misses. Orbit doesn't yet parse Dockerfiles (feature proposal issue #1416), so use that list to scope the code search in the next step, which confirms the base image and version in each project. You can also ask Orbit which projects have open findings for CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619 once scans have run. Orbit indexes the default branch only and is in beta for Premium and Ultimate on GitLab.com and GitLab Self-Managed.

3. Code search

Exact code search can find the two types of files that indicate a PHP project. Run these at the top-level group with regular expression mode enabled (the .* toggle at the right of the search box):

  • Container base images: This query searches for every file GitLab detects as a Dockerfile. The pattern matches any image whose name or tag contains php, so it also finds derivatives such as wordpress, frankenphp, or bitnami/php-fpm. Expect a few false positives that you can rule out by reading the result: lang:Dockerfile ^FROM.*php
  • Composer projects: This query finds projects that use PHP even when they have no Dockerfile, or when the Dockerfile takes its image from a build argument such as FROM $BASE_IMAGE:
file:composer\.json$

Exact code search covers the default branch only. On GitLab.com it is on by default for paid plans. On GitLab Self-Managed instances an administrator must install Zoekt first. GitLab Dedicated doesn't support exact code search.

For each result, confirm the version. You can check the FROM php: line, or run php -v in the running container, and compare it with the table above. The group dependency list shows Composer packages and framework versions but not the PHP runtime version.

4. Compare with your runtime inventory

Container scanning and code search show what your projects declare and build, not what runs. PHP can run outside your GitLab projects, for example on web servers with mod_php or PHP-FPM enabled only in their configuration, on hosts configured by hand, or in containers that still run in clusters without an active pipeline. Compare the static results with an inventory of your running workloads from your configuration management (Ansible, Puppet, Chef, etc.), cloud, or VM inventory tools. For Kubernetes, operational container scanning scans the images that run in your clusters, with the same package-only detection as container scanning. Treat every PHP runtime that appears in only one of the two views as a gap to investigate.

Remediate at scale with GitLab Duo Agent Platform

GitLab Duo can run the discovery steps above for you, across all your projects, through Orbit and code search. From there, let agents do the repetitive work and keep people on review and merge.

Automate the fix. Use Agentic Chat to create an epic with one issue per affected project and assign the Developer Flow to each. The flow opens a merge request that updates the base image tag or package to a fixed version. A flow trigger on the Assign event starts it the moment the issue is assigned. Turn on automatic reviews with the Code Review Flow to get a first review that follows your custom review instructions. Review and merge each merge request, then close the issue once the fixed version is deployed.

Enforce with policies. The merge request approval policy from Step 1 blocks any change that reintroduces a vulnerable PHP version without approval, and the scan execution policy keeps container scanning on in every project so a regression appears in the vulnerability report.

Searches find candidates, but a security or platform engineer still has to review each match, resolve CI includes, and tell what the code declares apart from what actually runs. An example agent skill from the GitLab Developer Advocacy team handles this work. It runs on GitLab Duo Agent Platform and with agents that use GitLab MCP server or the glab CLI, such as Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.

The skill checks container images, CI jobs, OS packages, configuration management variables, Composer pins, and environments. It returns a cited findings table with deployment evidence, and open gaps. The skill is read-only: It makes no changes, and remediation merge requests remain a separate, reviewed step. It cannot confirm what is running on hosts it cannot access, so verify those directly. Adapt the skill to your own environment before you use it.

Check for compromise

Reports of exploitation differ. Security researchers reported an exploit attempt on October 17, 2026, before public disclosure, and further reports of exploitation followed the release. The PHP project identified no functional exploits at the time of release. If an internet-facing server ran a vulnerable PHP version, review its logs from October 17, 2026, onward for:

  • Multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors or repeated HTTP 500 responses
  • Unusually large or malformed PHPSESSID response cookies
  • Unexplained PHP worker restarts, or shell processes started by PHP workers
  • Unexpected files on the PHP web server, outbound connections from PHP workers, or unexpected cron entries

A successful exploit can return HTTP 200 and leave the worker running, so an absence of errors doesn’t rule out compromise. If you find signs of exploitation, isolate the server and start an incident investigation. Where possible, capture memory, disk, and logs before patching and restarting. Restarting PHP workers may erase evidence. CVE-2026-109619 can also expose process memory, even when an attacker doesn’t achieve code execution. Rotate any credentials, tokens, or keys the PHP process could read.

Note: Scanners may flag the Gemnasium dependency scanning image (gemnasium:6), deprecated since GitLab 17.9, for its bundled PHP. It is used only as a command-line tool and never handles HTTP requests, so it is not exploitable, and a fixed version has already shipped under the same tag.

October 20Vulnerability details leak before coordinated disclosure. (Huntress)

Locate PHP projects across your GitLab groups

Any project that runs PHP to serve web requests needs a fixed version, including the ones that are easy to forget, such as an internal dashboard, a marketing site, or a CI job image. Finding them takes two views: a static search of what your repositories declare and your images contain, and a runtime inventory of what actually runs. GitLab covers the static view with three features. Use them in this order.

1. Container scanning

Container scanning reports vulnerabilities in operating system packages, so it finds PHP installed with apt, apk, or dnf, and it reports the two CVEs once they reach the scanner's vulnerability database. To turn it on for a project, add the template to .gitlab-ci.yml:

include:
  - template: Security/Container-Scanning.gitlab-ci.yml

container_scanning:
  variables:
    # Experimental, Ultimate only: also reports runtimes not installed by a package manager
    CS_BINARY_SCAN: "true"

You can also use a group-level scan execution policy to turn container scanning on for every project in a group at once. When a policy is enabled, the next time a pipeline is run, it will be run with container scanning. Container scanning results for the default branch can be reviewed in the Vulnerability Report after the scanner completes.

Additionally, you can set up Merge Request Approval policies with container scanning. With merge request approvals in play, if a code change contains PHP2Shell, the policy will block a merge without approval from the selected parties.

By default, container scanning detects only PHP installed as a package. The official images compile it from source, leaving no package record, so a project can pass container scanning and still run a vulnerable version.

Container scanning analyzer 8.7.0, released on October 29, adds an experimental binary scan that reports runtimes installed without a package manager, which closes that gap. It is available on Ultimate and off by default: set CS_BINARY_SCAN to "true" to turn it on. If you leave it off, Orbit and code search below cover it.

2. GitLab Orbit

GitLab Orbit indexes your projects, pipelines, security findings, and source code, including PHP, into a queryable graph, so you can ask an agent to review an entire group. With Orbit enabled on the top-level group, an agent can list every project that contains PHP code, including the projects that compile PHP or use the official php images, which container scanning misses. Orbit doesn't yet parse Dockerfiles (feature proposal issue #1416), so use that list to scope the code search in the next step, which confirms the base image and version in each project. You can also ask Orbit which projects have open findings for CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619 once scans have run. Orbit indexes the default branch only and is in beta for Premium and Ultimate on GitLab.com and GitLab Self-Managed.

3. Code search

Exact code search can find the two types of files that indicate a PHP project. Run these at the top-level group with regular expression mode enabled (the .* toggle at the right of the search box):

  • Container base images: This query searches for every file GitLab detects as a Dockerfile. The pattern matches any image whose name or tag contains php, so it also finds derivatives such as wordpress, frankenphp, or bitnami/php-fpm. Expect a few false positives that you can rule out by reading the result: lang:Dockerfile ^FROM.*php
  • Composer projects: This query finds projects that use PHP even when they have no Dockerfile, or when the Dockerfile takes its image from a build argument such as FROM $BASE_IMAGE:
file:composer\.json$

Exact code search covers the default branch only. On GitLab.com it is on by default for paid plans. On GitLab Self-Managed instances an administrator must install Zoekt first. GitLab Dedicated doesn't support exact code search.

For each result, confirm the version. You can check the FROM php: line, or run php -v in the running container, and compare it with the table above. The group dependency list shows Composer packages and framework versions but not the PHP runtime version.

4. Compare with your runtime inventory

Container scanning and code search show what your projects declare and build, not what runs. PHP can run outside your GitLab projects, for example on web servers with mod_php or PHP-FPM enabled only in their configuration, on hosts configured by hand, or in containers that still run in clusters without an active pipeline. Compare the static results with an inventory of your running workloads from your configuration management (Ansible, Puppet, Chef, etc.), cloud, or VM inventory tools. For Kubernetes, operational container scanning scans the images that run in your clusters, with the same package-only detection as container scanning. Treat every PHP runtime that appears in only one of the two views as a gap to investigate.

Remediate at scale with GitLab Duo Agent Platform

GitLab Duo can run the discovery steps above for you, across all your projects, through Orbit and code search. From there, let agents do the repetitive work and keep people on review and merge.

Automate the fix. Use Agentic Chat to create an epic with one issue per affected project and assign the Developer Flow to each. The flow opens a merge request that updates the base image tag or package to a fixed version. A flow trigger on the Assign event starts it the moment the issue is assigned. Turn on automatic reviews with the Code Review Flow to get a first review that follows your custom review instructions. Review and merge each merge request, then close the issue once the fixed version is deployed.

Enforce with policies. The merge request approval policy from Step 1 blocks any change that reintroduces a vulnerable PHP version without approval, and the scan execution policy keeps container scanning on in every project so a regression appears in the vulnerability report.

Searches find candidates, but a security or platform engineer still has to review each match, resolve CI includes, and tell what the code declares apart from what actually runs. An example agent skill from the GitLab Developer Advocacy team handles this work. Check for compromise

Reports of exploitation differ. Security researchers reported an exploit attempt on October 17, 2026, before public disclosure, and further reports of exploitation followed the release. The PHP project identified no functional exploits at the time of release. If an internet-facing server ran a vulnerable PHP version, review its logs from October 17, 2026, onward for:

  • Multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors or repeated HTTP 500 responses
  • Unusually large or malformed PHPSESSID response cookies
  • Unexplained PHP worker restarts, or shell processes started by PHP workers
  • Unexpected files on the PHP web server, outbound connections from PHP workers, or unexpected cron entries

A successful exploit can return HTTP 200 and leave the worker running, so an absence of errors doesn’t rule out compromise. If you find signs of exploitation, isolate the server and start an incident investigation. Where possible, capture memory, disk, and logs before patching and restarting. Restarting PHP workers may erase evidence. CVE-2026-109619 can also expose process memory, even when an attacker doesn’t achieve code execution. Rotate any credentials, tokens, or keys the PHP process could read.

Note: Scanners may flag the Gemnasium dependency scanning image (gemnasium:6), deprecated since GitLab 17.9, for its bundled PHP. It is used only as a command-line tool and never handles HTTP requests, so it is not exploitable, and a fixed version has already shipped under the same tag.
